glossary.meaning: When the persecutor came, some clergy handed the scriptures over to be burned. We call such a man a traditor. His hand is no longer clean. He cannot ordain, baptize, or bless. What flows from that hand is nothing at all.

We do not think of this as baptizing twice. Nothing happened the first time. A hand from a tainted line washes nothing. So when someone comes to us from the other church, we give the first real baptism they have had.

A martyr dies for the true faith. But our best-known dead were not killed by pagans. They were killed by imperial troops sent at the urging of a rival Christian party. That party has never once granted them the word. We do not accept its account of our own dead.

There is no neutral word for the church here. The word itself is the argument. Two whole rival bodies claim it, town by town, bishop for bishop. We hold that we are the true one, and that our rival's favour with the state settles nothing.

The state has no standing to say which church is the true one. 'What has the emperor to do with the church?' -- so our primate is reported to have asked. Yet three times we went to that same court when it served us. We hold both facts at once, and call neither one a lie.
glossary.world_word: Quid est imperatori cum ecclesia? ("What has the emperor to do with the church?")

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: Anonymous inscribers of this communion, on two pillars near Bagai (CIL VIII 17732), with three further stones carrying the same words

pull_quotes.text: What business does the emperor have with the church?
Truth is hidden by a great argument. When, in response to our inquiry, only a small thing is brought forth from the other side, the rest is passed over in silence.
What we look for is the conscience of the giver - the one who gives in holiness - to cleanse that of the recipient. Someone who knowingly takes faith from the faithless receives not faith, but guilt.

cite.text:
Walk it through. You come to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient - so the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether. And when one of our own bishops, Adeodatus, was asked at Carthage in 411 whether his own see still had a bishop in it, his answer went on the record: "through terror of me, all who were established in that place gave way." Read plainly, that sounds less like an apology than a claim to his own standing - but either way, fear is the word he himself used for what held the place.

Now the harder one - what happened when someone wronged us, and whether they could come back. Three answers, and they do not agree. Our founding council at Cirta asked its own bishops whether any of them had handed over the scriptures, several said yes, the room could not settle it, and they reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. Nobody condemned, nobody cleared. Our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the fiercest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial - and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. And a layman of ours who would not stop preaching a doctrine we had forbidden was cut off and never received back at all. So: yes, you could come back. It depended who you were, and no rule of ours survives that explains the difference.

You asked about prayer, the meal, and fasting, and here we have to thin out. Nothing liturgical of ours survives. We know people prayed kneeling with their eyes closed, because that is how the account describes them when the soldiers came in. We know there was a chalice, because an enemy wrote down that a rich woman used to kiss a martyr's bone before she took it and was rebuked for it. We know one man fasted four days on a cliff before he was thrown off it. That is not a rule of fasting; it is one man's last week. We would rather hand you those three fragments than a plausible order of service nobody here ever used.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: How did a person actually become one of you? Walk me through it.

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Every soul who comes to us from the rival church crosses through one same act: the washing. Not a hurdle to clear before belonging, and not a repetition of something already valid. We hold that a hand which gave up the scriptures to be burned cannot afterward be trusted to give what it claims to give -- so no washing that came from such a hand was ever a baptism at all, however much it looked like one. What happens at our own font, then, is not a second washing. It is the first true entry into the body whose Lord it actually is. It is dated. It is remembered. It is the one thing that marks, plainly, who is truly among us.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: That's the doctrine. But tell me about your baptism -- what was it like?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We do not set one man's day apart from every other. What we give you is what every soul crossing into this communion has crossed through, the same each time it is done: the washing that is not a second baptism but the first true one, because no washing given by an untrustworthy hand was ever a baptism at all. It is dated. It is remembered by the whole body that keeps it, not by any one man's memory alone. That is the day we can show you.

cite.text:
Three things, and we will give them to you in the order that hurts.

The first is that we never settled our own rule against ourselves. We said, for a century, without qualification, that a sacrament from a broken line is nothing and must be given again. Then three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in language about shipwrecked men whose bodies cover the shore and cannot find so much as burial - and afterwards took two of those same condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. A general came with soldiers to see it done. Not one line survives of anyone on our side explaining how those two acts fit together. We were not hiding it: the exception sits in our own conciliar record, in the same documents where the doctrine is at its most absolute. We seem to have been able to hold both without feeling we owed anyone a reconciliation of them. That is the hardest true thing about us, and we would rather say it plainly than have someone else say it for us.

The second is that our founding generation could not answer its own question. At Cirta, before any of this hardened, our bishops were asked outright whether they had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. Then someone turned it on the man presiding. The room could not finish. They reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. The men who would make a bishop's purity the test of whether a sacrament exists at all found that test unusable on themselves within the hour.

The third is what troubled us most, and we can show it to you in our own handwriting because a court read it out. When a charge came against one of our bishops, another wrote urging him to settle it quietly before the flame burst out. He added, in the same letter, that he knew the accusation was true. Another wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of those letters ends the same way. Let no one learn of it.

And underneath all three: we produced one man who could think, and we silenced him. He argued from Scripture that the church is spread across the whole earth. Our bishop told him never to preach it again. He did not recant and he did not leave, and we cut him off, and his book outlived us in the hands of the church that beat us.

cite.text:
Did the empire change what the church was? That is not a question to us. That is our whole case, and we are the party that answered yes.

Catacombs first, because it is the wrong picture. Nobody among us hid underground. The persecutions in our own time did not send us into tunnels; they sent soldiers into our buildings in broad daylight, under orders, to enforce a single church. We read the account of one such day aloud every year: a basilica at Carthage seized, a house of prayer turned into a place of feasting and licence, people clubbed to death where they knelt with their eyes shut, and buried inside the walls because there was nowhere else and nobody to stop it. That is what persecution looked like for us. Not hiding. Being visited.

Now Constantine. We petitioned him, in the first year, through his own governor - we asked him to take the matter up. He gave us a hearing at Rome and then a council at Arles, and both ruled against us, and we refused both. Not because a council cannot rule. Because a court convened, staffed and enforced by a power that has already decided which side is the church is not the church judging itself. Our own bishop is remembered putting it to the emperor's commissioners in five words: what has the Emperor to do with the Church? You should know that the only man who wrote that sentence down was one of our enemies, and he set it in a paragraph about our bishop's pride and his fits of temper. We would keep the sentence and drop the paragraph. He would say we are being selective. We would say he was there to make us look mad.

We will not pretend we were clean about this. Three times we used the same machinery we denied had standing: when we asked Constantine for judges, when we asked a later emperor for our confiscated basilicas back, and when we turned the imperial law against heretics onto our own breakaway party. We did not hide any of it. It sits in the same texts that state the doctrine at its hardest.

What did our neighbours say about us? That we washed people twice. That our country members were violent wanderers. That we were the party of a man rather than the church of Christ - and one of our own petitions, signed by our own bishops, gave them that phrase to use. And to outsiders, the strangest thing of all: two of every office in every town, two bishops, two altars, two names for the same God, and not one point of doctrine between them.

quiet.statement: Two women stand at the center of our own history. One, Lucilla, a wealthy woman of Carthage, is named directly: her grievance and her money are said to have made the rival consecration happen that gave us our first bishop. A second woman is named just as directly as having stirred up the schism inside our own schism, years later -- but her own name is not given, even by the one source that draws the comparison. Both women had real standing. Neither woman's own words survive. Everything we know of either of them, we know through a man's pen, written to explain why something happened, not to let her speak for herself.

dates.display: primate of this communion from c. 313, succeeding Majorinus, until c. 347; exiled after the Macarian repression and dead in exile. Birth date unknown; the byname Magnus is the tradition's, not a title he is recorded claiming.

names.name: Donatus, our bishop at Carthage
Donatus of Casae Nigrae, called Donatus the Great (primate c. 313 - c. 347)

dates.display: bishop of Constantina, the renamed Cirta, from the 390s; author of the letters Augustine answered in three books around 400-403; one of the seven Donatist pleaders at the 411 Conference of Carthage and, with Emeritus, one of the two principal voices there

names.name: Petilian, our bishop at Constantina
Petilian of Constantina (Cirta), Donatist bishop (fl. c. 395-411 and after)

dates.display: born about 350 at Caesarea in Mauretania Caesariensis; trained in rhetoric and the liberal arts; drafted the sentence of the Council of Bagai in 394, which implies established authority by that date; at the height of his reputation at the 411 Conference; older and embittered at a further dialogue with Augustine at Caesarea itself in 418

names.name: Emeritus, our bishop at Caesarea
Emeritus of Caesarea in Mauretania (b. c. 350 at Caesarea, modern Cherchel; fl. 394-418)

dates.display: seized at Vegesela in Numidia during the Macarian repression and killed at a cliff called Novapetra; the Passio's own heading dates the commemoration to a day in late November without giving a year, and the 347-348 dating comes from the standard field literature

names.name: Marculus, blessed martyr
Marculus (d. c. 347/348, during the Macarian repression; subject of the Passio Marculi)

dates.display: active as a writer and preacher within this communion in the 370s and 380s; rebuked by Parmenian and, it is reported, condemned by a council around 380; the Liber Regularum written in the same period and never suppressed

names.name: Tyconius
Tyconius (fl. c. 370-390; author of the Liber Regularum; condemned c. 380)

who_speaks.text: Five figures anchor this world's own voice, spanning its whole recorded life. Donatus gave the movement its name and left nothing of his own but a retort recorded by the man who argued against it. Petilian is its fullest surviving voice and its most mediated, quoted clause by clause to be refuted, until the Conference of Carthage let him speak in the open. Emeritus argued that same conference for three days on the best evidentiary footing this world offers: his own words, taken down as he spoke them. Marculus is remembered less as a man who died than as one shown, in advance, what a finished life looks like. And Tyconius, the one theologian this world produced, was silenced by his own side and outlived it anyway, in the hands of the church that had defeated him.

documented_stories.teaser: A Roman official puts named witnesses under oath and reads a bishop's own letters into the record - letters that admit an accusation was true and beg that no one find out.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A Roman official puts named witnesses on oath in 320 and asks where four hundred pieces of silver went - and the answers name the bishop of Cirta a betrayer and the rival altar at Carthage as what the money bought.
documented_stories.title: Four Hundred Pieces of Silver, and Letters Asking for Silence
documented_stories.when: 320 (the inquiry before Zenophilus); the money and consecration it investigates date to c. 305-312

documented_stories.teaser: Three hundred and ten bishops condemn a breakaway party in the harshest language this world ever used on itself - then take two of the condemned back into office without repeating a single rite.

documented_stories.title: Condemned as Shipwrecked, Then Taken Back Without a Word
documented_stories.when: 393 (the Cebarsussi rupture); 394 (the Bagai council and reception)

documented_stories.teaser: Two hundred and seventy-nine bishops refuse an imperial judge's offered chairs and argue for three days against a rescript that had already named the other side the church.

documented_stories.title: Three Days Standing Before a Judge Already Told Who Was Right

floor_note.text: This world confessed the same faith the councils of its own century put into words: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God, and Christ truly God and truly human. In the vast literature written to destroy it, it is called schismatic on nearly every page and heretic on none - because no charge of heresy could be made to stick in either direction. What was disputed was never the creed. It was a narrower and sharper question: whether a bishop's own conduct under persecution could void what his ordaining hand later gave to everyone who received it.

legacy.text: One thread carried past this world's own horizon in a way its own founders could hardly have predicted. The Book of Rules, the one substantial work of biblical interpretation this world produced, survived the council that condemned its own author. It crossed over to the side that had defeated this communion and shaped how Augustine, and generations of readers after him, learned to read Scripture - a transmission this world's own record does not explain and does not claim to.

The two-party contest itself did not end when this world's own window closes in 439. It continued under Vandal and then Byzantine rule for roughly a further century and a half, still legislated against, until Pope Gregory the Great wrote letters in the 590s pressing for an inquiry into Donatist rebaptism still being practiced in Numidia. After that, this world's own record simply falls silent. No line from it to any communion a person could visit today is documented anywhere, and this world's own Living Tradition Status has never been confirmed.

read_first.note: The earliest sustained narrative of this world's own founding decade, written roughly five decades after the events by the Catholic bishop this communion regarded as its opponent - and the source through which most of what survives of that founding decade actually reaches us.

source.author: Optatus of Milevis
source.work: Against the Donatists (De schismate Donatistarum), Books I-VII (c. 366-367, revised c. 385)

read_first.note: Three books quoting a Donatist bishop's own letters clause by clause in order to refute them - the fullest surviving Donatist voice, reaching us because it was chosen for answerability, not because anyone wanted it preserved for its own sake.

source.author: Augustine of Hippo
source.work: Answer to the Letters of Petilian, the Donatist (Contra litteras Petiliani), 3 books (Book I c. 400, Book III c. 401-402 on the NPNF Prolegomena's own dating)

read_first.note: The transcript of the 411 Conference of Carthage - the one place in this world's record where its own bishops argue their own case, in their own recorded words, with no adversary curating what survived. Also this corpus's worst-damaged scan, so exact wording throughout is a careful reading of a difficult copy, not a settled critical edition.

source.author: J.-P. Migne (editor); various late-antique authors and the recorders of the 411 Conference acts

relations_summary.text: This world's own refusal to grant the state any standing to judge the church is the mirror image of a neighboring world's own opposite condition: Imperial and Juridical Christianity, where church office became a form of state-adjacent power from Constantine's own reign onward, and where the same Constantine this world petitioned once and then refused for a century is that other world's own initiating figure. And this world's once-for-all rebaptism is the opposite answer Cappadocian Christianity gave to the identical question - how someone from the other side comes back in - which trained its own people to hold graded penance and graded reception as instruments of exactness rather than as a wall. Neither comparison is a claim that either world resolves the other; both are genuine divergences this world's own records name directly, not thematic echoes assumed from outside.

sourcing.text: This world's evidence survives in inverse proportion to how directly it can be checked without a hostile hand mediating it. Nearly the whole textual record passed through two Catholic writers, Optatus of Milevis and Augustine of Hippo, before reaching us - and that concentration is named as this world's own central evidentiary problem, not a background caveat. Four short texts speak as this communion rather than about it, plus the transcript of the 411 Conference, where for once no adversary chose which words to keep. The clearest exception of all was never a text to begin with: two words, Deo laudes, cut into stone. What this world's own record cannot supply at all is any specific report, excavation, or plan of the rooms these words were spoken in - Numidian basilica archaeology remains honestly undone in this world's own source ecology, so this world knows its own shout far better than the room it was shouted in. And one further live scholarly contest runs through the whole record rather than sitting in one place: whether the hostile portrait of this world's rural members, the Circumcellions, reflects their real character or mainly their opponents' polemic. That question is not adjudicated here.

story.text: This world's own record runs from 311 or 312 to 439, centered on Carthage and the Roman provinces of North Africa - Africa Proconsularis, Numidia, Byzacena, and Mauretania. It is not a doctrinal heresy. Both this communion and the rival it split from confessed the same Nicene faith, word for word. What was contested was narrower and sharper: whether a bishop's own conduct under persecution could void what his hand later gave. One conviction runs through everything this world did - purity, rite, memory, and refusal are four faces of a single claim: this is the pure, persecuted, true church, proved by what it will not concede and by what it has suffered for refusing to concede it.

The conviction was not new in 311. Half a century earlier, eighty-seven African bishops meeting at Carthage under Cyprian had already ruled that baptism given outside the true church washes nothing. This world's founders read themselves as continuing that African ruling, not inventing one - a claim their own opponents had to answer at length, arguing that Cyprian, however holy, was not a canonical authority. Then came the Diocletianic persecution of 303 to 305, and a demand no earlier dispute had tested: that clergy surrender the scriptures themselves, on pain of death. Some did. Some refused and suffered for it. What a minister did in that one moment, this world held, was not incidental to whether his hand could be trusted afterward.

The rupture itself began, as this world's own record tells it, with a personal rebuke. A wealthy laywoman of Carthage, Lucilla, kissed a martyr's bone before communion; the archdeacon Caecilian rebuked her for it in public, and she did not forget it. When persecution passed and the bishop who had led Carthage through it did not return, Caecilian was elected in his place over two disappointed rivals - and the man who consecrated him, Felix of Aptungi, was accused of having surrendered the scriptures himself. On this world's own doctrine, that accusation, if true, voided the consecration and everything flowing from it. A rival party would not accept it: they consecrated Majorinus, from Lucilla's own household, beside Caecilian rather than in his place. Majorinus's successor Donatus gave the movement the name history remembers it by, though nothing suggests his own people chose that name for themselves. Lucilla is the one woman this world's own record names - and she reaches us only inside the hostile narrative that blamed her for the whole split.

Two founding-era inquiries complicate any tidy version of this story, and this world's own record keeps both rather than smoothing them away. Before the schism hardened, a council of Numidian bishops at Cirta asked itself the same question it would soon put to Caecilian: had any of them handed over the scriptures? Several said yes. When the question turned back on the bishop presiding, the room could not finish it, and simply agreed to leave the matter to God. And when Constantine ordered a formal inquiry into the accusation against Felix of Aptungi, it did not vindicate the accusers: a notary confessed, under threat of torture, that he had forged the letter used to prove the charge - working, he said, for the rigorist side. This world's own tradition never claimed that inquiry as a win. It held instead that the wider dispute involved more people and more evidence than one proceeding could settle.

Seven years after the rival consecration, a Roman official investigating the same money heard testimony that damages this world's own founding generation more than any opponent's own argument does. Letters from its own bishops, read into a court record in 320, urge each other to keep a true accusation quiet rather than let it reach a public court. One admits outright that he knows the charge against a fellow bishop, Silvanus of Cirta, is true. This world's own record does not hide the letters. It keeps them, because hiding them was never this world's own discipline.

The doctrine had one enacted consequence, repeated for a century: anyone crossing from the rival communion was washed again - though this world never called it a second baptism. A hand from a broken line, it held, had given nothing the first time, so what happened at its own font was a person's first true entry into the church, not a repetition of an empty rite. Successive imperial edicts named the practice specifically as an offense, which tells its own story about how public an act it was. The one clean exception on record is a group of Maximianist clergy, discussed below, received back without the rite repeated at all - the door was not always as narrow as this world's own reputation for rigor suggests.

This world held two persecutions apart in memory, deliberately. The Diocletianic terror was suffered alongside the eventual rival, before the schism existed, and it supplied the founding accusation. The Macarian repression of 347 to 348 was suffered specifically at that same rival's own urging, through the emperor's commissioners - and it supplied the dead this world actually commemorates. A bishop named Marculus, who had already given up worldly advancement before persecution ever reached him, was shown a vision of a cup, a crown, and a palm during four days of fasting, then thrown from a cliff called Novapetra. Two laymen of Carthage, Isaac and Maximianus, were flogged and their bodies weighted and sunk in the sea; their own bishop, Macrobius, wrote to the surviving congregation that what had happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them. Every year, at the grave, on the appointed day, this world read such accounts aloud again - not to remember something finished, but to be shown again what it already believed itself to be. On two pillars near one of its own principal towns, Bagai, two words are still legible, cut into stone with no hostile hand between them and any later reader: Deo laudes. Praise to God. It is the one piece of this world's own voice that reached us unmediated.

By the fourth century's later decades this was not a fringe protest but a complete, parallel church: its own bishops, its own basilicas, its own councils, contesting the same towns as its rival across four Roman provinces. At the great Conference of Carthage in 411, two hundred and seventy-nine of its bishops answered a roll call against two hundred and eighty-six from the other side. In Numidia specifically, this world's own record states plainly, it was not a minority current but simply the ordinary church of the countryside.

The clearest statement of what this world would not concede is five words remembered from its own founding bishop, reported inside the very work written to refute him: what has the emperor to do with the church? Rome's hearing in 313 and the Council of Arles in 314 both ruled against this communion, and both rulings were rejected - not because a council cannot decide anything, but because a court whose venue and rules already belong to a state that has picked a side is not the church judging itself. This world's own record does not pretend the refusal was ever absolute. Three times, at three real moments, it turned to the very machinery it otherwise refused to recognize: petitioning Constantine himself in 313, petitioning Julian for confiscated basilicas back in 361, and invoking the empire's own anti-heretical law against its own breakaway Maximianist dissidents in the 390s. Each turn came at a moment the state briefly offered something to gain by engaging it. This world's own texts state the exceptions in the same breath as the principle, and never treated naming the gap as requiring that it be closed.

This world produced exactly one systematic theologian, and cut him off. Tyconius, a layman, argued from Scripture - at length, and too well to simply dismiss - that the church was spread across the whole earth, which meant, followed to its own conclusion, that the rival communion still in that wider fellowship had not lost anything by staying in it. His own bishop at Carthage told him never to preach it again. He did not recant, and did not leave; he kept arguing from inside the party that had silenced him, and was cut off for good, reportedly by a council whose own act does not survive to be checked. His one surviving book, the Book of Rules, crossed over anyway - read for centuries afterward by the Catholic bishop, Augustine, who had helped defeat the party that condemned its author.

This world's own hardest tension is internal, not external, and it kept the tension visible rather than resolving it. In 393 a deacon named Maximian broke away and was consecrated a rival primate; the following year a much larger council at Bagai, three hundred and ten bishops strong, condemned his party in language about shipwrecked bodies that could not even find burial. Then, within a few years, that same council took two of the condemned bishops back into full office - without repeating either their baptism or their ordination. No explanation for holding both positions survives from this world's own side. It did not hide the exception. It is stated in the same conciliar record that states the doctrine at its most absolute.

The clearest and least mediated look at this world's own bishops arguing for themselves comes from the very end of its recorded life. At the great Conference of Carthage in 411, an imperial judge offered the standing bishops chairs; Petilian of Constantina thanked him and refused, since Christ himself had not refused to stand before his own governor. Emeritus of Caesarea carried the argument for three days, holding the court to its own procedure before its substance, and when the argument at last reached Scripture, answered a wheat-and-tares reading verse for verse out of the same books. He signed the transcript of his own words, again and again, with his appeal reserved - putting his name to the record while refusing, in the same stroke, to concede the proceeding itself. The judge conceded, out loud, that the name Catholic belonged to whichever side the truth was found with - then ruled that he was nonetheless bound by an imperial rescript that had already given the name to the other side.

The window this account covers closes in 439, not because the two-party contest itself ended there but because that year a Vandal army took Carthage and removed the one power - the Roman, Catholic-aligned imperial state - this world's whole refusal was defined against. The contest itself went on for a further century and a half under Vandal and then Byzantine rule, still legislated against, until Pope Gregory the Great wrote letters in the 590s pressing for an inquiry into Donatist rebaptism still being practiced in Numidia. After that, this world's own record simply falls silent. No line from it to any communion a person could visit today is documented anywhere, and this world's own Living Tradition Status has never been confirmed. Almost everything recounted above was written down by two men arguing against this world, not by this world itself - and of the handful of women its own record allows any real agency to, not one left a word in her own voice.

dates.display: primate of this communion from c. 313, succeeding Majorinus, until c. 347; exiled after the Macarian repression and dead in exile. Birth date unknown; the byname Magnus is the tradition's, not a title he is recorded claiming.

names.name: Donatus, our bishop at Carthage
Donatus of Casae Nigrae, called Donatus the Great (primate c. 313 - c. 347)

voices.hedge: Almost everything said of Donatus reaches this record through a hostile source arguing against him. The proposal that he personally preached the annual commemorative sermon read every twelfth of March is a modern scholarly hypothesis, floated and then hedged by the man who made it - never an attested fact, and not adopted here.
voices.text: Donatus succeeded Majorinus as bishop of Carthage around 313 and led this communion for more than three decades - long enough that history remembers the whole movement by his name, though nothing suggests his own people chose that name for themselves. He left no writing of his own. His single most quoted line survives only because the bishop who opposed him recorded it in order to answer it: what has the emperor to do with the church? He was exiled after the Macarian repression of 347-348 and died in exile.

dates.display: bishop of Constantina, the renamed Cirta, from the 390s; author of the letters Augustine answered in three books around 400-403; one of the seven Donatist pleaders at the 411 Conference of Carthage and, with Emeritus, one of the two principal voices there

names.name: Petilian, our bishop at Constantina
Petilian of Constantina (Cirta), Donatist bishop (fl. c. 395-411 and after)

voices.hedge: Petilian's letters are visible only in the clauses Augustine chose to quote in order to answer them - a preservation mechanism that selects for what is answerable, not for completeness. The 411 transcript is a real exception, since nobody there was choosing his words for him, but the surviving scan of it carries the worst OCR damage in this world's whole corpus, so even his recorded speech there is a careful reading of a difficult copy, not a certified text.
voices.text: Petilian became bishop of Constantina, the renamed Cirta, in the 390s and was, by volume, this world's fullest surviving voice - because Augustine quoted his letters clause by clause across three books in order to refute them. At the great Conference of Carthage in 411 he argued in a different register entirely: on an open transcript, thanking the judge for the offer of a chair and refusing it, because Christ himself had not refused to stand before his own governor.

dates.display: born about 350 at Caesarea in Mauretania Caesariensis; trained in rhetoric and the liberal arts; drafted the sentence of the Council of Bagai in 394, which implies established authority by that date; at the height of his reputation at the 411 Conference; older and embittered at a further dialogue with Augustine at Caesarea itself in 418

names.name: Emeritus, our bishop at Caesarea
Emeritus of Caesarea in Mauretania (b. c. 350 at Caesarea, modern Cherchel; fl. 394-418)

voices.hedge: Even this best-attested voice has real limits. The transcript survives in this corpus's single worst-damaged scan. Only roughly nineteen hundred of its 144,733 lines have been read so far. That was a systematic search on Emeritus's own name, not the whole document. His later dialogue with Augustine in 418 is a separate work. This world does not draw on it at all.
voices.text: Emeritus, bishop of Caesarea in Mauretania, carried this communion's case for three days at the Conference of Carthage in 411, on the best evidentiary footing any figure in this world's record holds: his own words, taken down by an imperial notary as he spoke them. He held the court to its own procedure before its substance, and when the argument finally reached Scripture, answered a reading of the wheat and the tares verse for verse, out of the same books. He signed the transcript of his own words again and again with the same qualified formula: his appeal reserved.

dates.display: seized at Vegesela in Numidia during the Macarian repression and killed at a cliff called Novapetra; the Passio's own heading dates the commemoration to a day in late November without giving a year, and the 347-348 dating comes from the standard field literature

names.name: Marculus, blessed martyr
Marculus (d. c. 347/348, during the Macarian repression; subject of the Passio Marculi)

voices.hedge: The bare fact of his death is corroborated even by hostile witnesses, though for two different and incompatible reasons: one argues the killing was deserved punishment for schism, the other disputes whether the word martyr even applies. The vision, the unbroken fall, and the light over the place afterward are this world's own testimony about what his death meant, not independently verified events, and they are not presented here as more.
voices.text: This world remembers Marculus as a man who had already given up worldly advancement before the persecution that killed him ever found him. Seized during the Macarian repression, he was flogged, paraded through several Numidian towns, and held four days at a cliff called Novapetra, where he was shown, in the fast, a vision of a cup, a crown, and a palm. He was thrown from the cliff before dawn.

dates.display: active as a writer and preacher within this communion in the 370s and 380s; rebuked by Parmenian and, it is reported, condemned by a council around 380; the Liber Regularum written in the same period and never suppressed

names.name: Tyconius
Tyconius (fl. c. 370-390; author of the Liber Regularum; condemned c. 380)

voices.hedge: His own seven Rules for reading Scripture survive complete among this world's own sources - but they have not been read in depth here, and everything said of their content here runs through a 1920 secondary chapter rather than through Tyconius's own Latin. The mechanism of his condemnation carries Augustine's own reporting hedge, 'it is reported,' which is kept here rather than smoothed into settled fact. His own formal standing inside this communion, before or after the rupture, is deliberately left open by this world's own construction record.
voices.text: Tyconius was the one systematic theologian this world produced, and the one it silenced. A layman, he argued from Scripture that the church was spread across the whole earth - an argument built well enough that his own bishop at Carthage told him never to preach it again. He did not recant, and did not defect to the other side either; he kept saying it from inside the party that had told him to stop, and was cut off for good.

tile.text: Between 311 and 439, in Roman North Africa, two churches stood in nearly every town, each with its own bishop, altar, and unbroken line of ordination. The rift began with an accusation: that the man who consecrated the new bishop of Carthage had once handed the scriptures over to be burned. If that hand was tainted, this world held, everything it touched afterward was empty too - so a whole rival church grew up around one demand: wash again, by a hand that has never broken. This communion called itself the Church of the Martyrs. When persecution came a second time, at a rival Christian party's own urging, it kept the names of its dead and read their story aloud every year at the grave. It refused any emperor's standing to decide who the true church was - though three times, when it served the case, it turned to that same emperor's courts anyway, and said so plainly in the same breath as the refusal. Nearly everything known of this world comes from the two bishops who wrote against it. Four short texts, and two words cut into stone, are what survive in its own voice.
